newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Waigel defends his position on gold battle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Waigel defends his position on gold battle.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Thursday rejected calls to resign over his controversial plan to revalue Germany's gold and currency reserves and insisted the revaluation was a necessary step.

Waigel, speaking at a hastily-convened news briefing in his home region of Bavaria, told reporters "not a single mark" of the proceeds would go to reduce Germany's budget deficit, which experts say could keep Germany out European monetary union.
"Germany can meet the EMU criteria even without the reserve revaluation," Waigel told journalists, adding that the move was nonetheless necessary ahead of the start of currency union.

EU nations wanting to join the first wave of monetary union must, according to the Maastricht Treaty, have a 1997 budget deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a debt of no more than 60 percent of GDP.
Waigel is under pressure to find ways to plug deficit and debt problems, which includes tapping the Bundesbank reserves but has drawn fierce criticism from the financial community.
Waigel brushed off calls from opposition politicians for his resignation following the Bundesbank's rejection of his plan on Wednesday to book the reserves towards market prices.
Rudolf Scharping, parliamentary leader of the Social Democrats (SPD) told Thursday's Berliner Zeitung, that Waigel should quit, saying: "The man is no longer tolerable".
"I hear calls for my resignation every day. But I have been in office for eight years and I am used to them," Waigel said, adding he was "very at ease" about his eight years in office.

Waigel said the proceeds from the revaluation would flow step by step into a fund created to offset long-term debt, something he said the central bank had in principle accepted as possible from 1999, the planned start-date for currency union.

He found support from Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary leader of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, telling Reuters in an interview the revaluation was a better option than heading for a loose interpretation of entry criteria.
The Bundesbank opposes making the payment before the currency union's start because it believes such a move would undermine its credibility.
German politicians and the press on Thursday poured hefty criticism on Waigel for insisting that they would override the respected central bank and its opposition to the revaluation.

One Bundesbank council member, Ernst Welteke, warned Chancellor Helmut Kohl that he had failed to win public support for his pet project and that the Bundesbank would command more public sympathy than politicians in a clash.
"Politicians do not have a great deal of credit with the public at the moment," Welteke said in an interview late on Wednesday with German radio.

Financial experts also denounced the grab for gold as a threat to the euro currency Bonn wants to launch on schedule on January 1, 1999 and said Waigel's plan undermined the credibility of the future currency.

"The Bundesbank statement represents a huge slap in the face for Waigel and sets the stage for an open conflict with the government," said Holger Fahrinkrug, an economist at Union Bank of Switzerland in Frankfurt.
German financial markets got a small scare from the clash.
The dollar surged more than a pfennig against the mark in European dealings and German debt prices slumped in London trade since the Frankfurt market was closed for a holiday.
The U.S. currency eased slightly on Waigel's defence of the plan, while Bunds steadied.

The open split with the Bundesbank adds clear domestic political risks to Bonn's troubles. Kohl has the majority in Bonn to make the necessary law changes to allow the revaluation and opposition politicians attacked his decision to use political power to get his way.
